en: The Buddha Preaches the Sūtra on the Extinction of the Dharma.
(In the *Sengyou lu*, the translator’s name is lost; it is now appended to the Song dynasty records.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī—where the Tathāgata was to remain for three months.
The Parinirvāṇa— [occurred] as innumerable hosts of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrating themselves upon the ground.
The World-Honored One remained in tranquil silence, saying nothing, and his radiance did not manifest.
The worthy Ānanda paid homage and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, in the past and present, the majestic radiance of your preaching of the Dharma has been uniquely manifest; yet now, in this great assembly, that light does not appear. For what reason is this so?"
"There must be a reason for this; I wish to hear its meaning.
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond, and this was repeated up to three times.
Then the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be an age of the five heinous crimes and the turbid world where the paths of Māra flourish.
Māras will take the form of śramaṇas to corrupt and disrupt my Way; they will don the garments of the laity, taking pleasure in *kāṣāya* robes and clothing of the five colors;
they will drink wine and eat meat, killing living beings out of greed for flavor."
Lacking any heart of compassion, they instead harbored mutual hatred and jealousy.

At that time, there were bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats who cultivated virtue through diligent effort; all paid them respect and honor, and they were those toward whom people looked for guidance.
They taught with impartiality, taking pity on the poor and keeping the elderly in mind, nurturing those who were destitute and in distress.
He constantly had others venerate scriptures and images to cultivate various meritorious deeds;
his disposition was kind and virtuous, and he never harmed others.
He sacrificed his own body to save sentient beings, cherishing himself not at all, and was patient, harmonious, and benevolent.
Should there be such a person, the bhikṣus who are Māras will all become envious of him; they will slander and spread his ill repute, expelling and driving him away so that he may not remain.
Thereafter, they themselves will no longer cultivate the Way or its virtue; the temples will fall into ruin and desolation, no longer being repaired but instead continuing toward decay.
They will merely covet wealth and goods, accumulating them without dispersing them, and fail to perform meritorious deeds.
They trade in slaves, cultivate fields and plant crops, burn down mountains and forests, and harm living beings without a heart of compassion;

when male slaves become bhikṣus and female slaves become bhikṣuṇīs, they lack morality and virtue, becoming licentious and turbidly chaotic, with no distinction between male and female, thereby causing the Way to become thin and diluted—all because of such as these.
Some, seeking to escape the local authorities, take refuge in my Way and request ordination as śramaṇas, yet they do not cultivate the precepts and rules;

though they recite the precepts at the beginning and end of each month, they are weary and indolent, having no desire to listen, and they abridge the beginning and end of the text, refusing to recite it in its entirety;

they do not study or practice the sūtras, and even if there are those who read them, they do not understand the characters or phrases, yet they insist on speaking as if they did, without consulting those who are wise.
Arrogant and seeking fame, they falsely display elegant deportment as a source of glory, hoping for offerings from others.

After these bhikṣus of the Māras pass away, their spirits shall fall into the Avīci Hell; among the five heinous crimes, there is no rebirth as a hungry ghost or an animal that they will not undergo. Only after the end of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will their retribution be exhausted, at which point they will emerge to be born in a borderland where the Three Jewels do not exist.
"When the Dharma is about to perish, women will be diligent and constantly perform meritorious deeds;
men will be indolent and arrogant, disregarding the words of the Dharma. They will look upon śramaṇas as they would dung and soil, possessing no faith."
When the Dharma is on the verge of extinction, at that time the devas weep tears.
Water and drought will be不调 (irregular), the five grains will not ripen, pestilence will spread, and those who die will be numerous.
The people toil and suffer while the officials calculate and exact taxes; not conforming to the Way, they all long for chaos.
Evil people increase like the sands of the sea, while the good are exceedingly few—perhaps only one or two.

As the kalpa draws to a close, the days and months grow shorter and the lifespan of humans becomes increasingly brief; by the age of forty, men’s hair turns white, their vital essence is exhausted, and they meet an untimely death, with some living only to sixty years.
The lifespan of men is short, while that of women is long—reaching seventy, eighty, ninety, or even a hundred years.
When a great flood suddenly arises and arrives without warning, people do not believe it and thus regard such things as permanent.
Sentient beings of various kinds, regardless of their noble or lowly status, were submerged and drifting about, being devoured by fish and turtles.
At that time, there were bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats whom the various māras drove away so that they were not permitted to join the assembly.
The Three Vehicles shall enter this mountain, a land of merit, where they may dwell in tranquility and self-restraint, finding joy therein and extending their lifespans.
Protected by the various devas, they shall encounter the appearance of Candraprabha in the world; together they shall promote my Way for fifty-two years.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* and the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* were first extinguished; subsequently, the twelve divisions of the scriptures were also completely extinguished and no longer appear.
"One will no longer see written texts, and the saffron robes of the śramaṇas will naturally turn white.

When my Dharma is extinguished, it will be like an oil lamp that, as it is about to go out, its light becomes even more intense before it finally extinguishes; the extinction of my Dharma will be just like the extinguishing of that lamp."
From this point forward, it would be difficult to recount them all.
After such a period of many tens of millions of years, Maitreya shall descend to the world and become a Buddha.

The world will be in great peace, poisonous vapors will be eliminated, rains will fall with harmonious moderation, the five grains will flourish, and trees will grow tall. Humans will be eight *zhang* in height and all will live for eighty-four thousand years; the number of sentient beings who attain deliverance will be beyond calculation.
The venerable Ānanda paid homage and addressed the Buddha:
"What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! This sutra is named ‘The Extinction of the Dharma.’”
"Declare all things; you should cause them to be distinguished, for their merit is immeasurable and beyond calculation.

When the disciples of the fourfold assembly heard this sutra, they were moved by grief and despondency; they all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, holy, and true path, and having paid homage to the Buddha, they departed.
The Buddha Preaches the Sūtra on the Extinction of the Dharma.
